name: AIntern
purpose: an AI intern for any team
intro: Office work is full of forms, checks and sign-offs. In AIntern, a person describes the work in plain words, and an agent builds it as a workflow on a live canvas.
The agent tests each step as it adds it. Where the result matters, a review stops the run until a person reads it and approves.
Each organisation runs its own instance, with its own accounts, rules and budget.

sections.title: How it works
body: A workflow goes through 5 steps. People do the first and the fourth, the agent does the 2 between them, and the last one repeats for as long as the work does.

wide: a person     the agent    the agent    a person     a trigger
in words     on canvas    each step    signs off    or button
figure.alt: Five steps in a row: a person says the work in words, the agent builds it on the canvas, the agent tests each step, a person signs off, and a trigger or a button runs it.

steps.label: Say
steps.text: You describe the work in the chat, as you would to a new colleague.

steps.label: Build
steps.text: The agent adds nodes to the canvas and connects them.

steps.label: Test
steps.text: It runs each step with real input and fixes what fails.

steps.label: Review
steps.text: The run stops here until the named person approves.

steps.label: Run
steps.text: From then on a schedule, a form or a button starts it.

sections.title: Build
body: You say what the work is, in the chat beside the canvas or from your own agent over MCP. Nodes appear on the canvas as the agent adds them.
Technical choices are the agent's. Business rules are yours: who approves, what counts as an exception, who is told. When a rule is open, the agent asks in a card and waits for the answer.
Every change is a version, so an earlier state is one step back.

figure.alt: The chat adds three steps to a workflow on the canvas, then reports its test.

sections.title: Nodes
body: A workflow is a graph of 10 kinds of node. Rules that must give the same answer every time go in Python. Models only read and write text.

points.text: Says how the workflow starts and what it takes in.
Runs a function in a sandbox, with files, a browser or office documents.
A model reads and writes, at one of 3 tiers, with tools and web search if it needs them.
Stops the run until the named people approve.
Sends the run one way or another by a rule.
Runs the steps after it once per item in a list.
Pauses for a duration or until a time.
Keeps rows from one run to the next.
Reads and writes Docs, Sheets and Slides.
Returns the result, sends it, fills a form or publishes a page.

sections.title: Review
body: A review goes before any step that changes something for people: a form submitted for someone, mail to the outside, money.
The reviewers are people or groups, and the rule is any of them, all of them or a count. A reviewer can correct the data, or send the run back to an earlier step with a comment.
Only a person in a browser can approve. The agent cannot, and neither can a token or an MCP client.

figure.alt: A review card shows a leave request with Send back and Approve, above the workflow that waits on it.

sections.title: Starts and ends
body: A workflow starts 5 ways and ends 5 ways. The same workflow can sit behind a form for the whole office, or run every Monday at 9.

wide: a person presses Run ─╮                  ╭─ a result page
an incoming webhook ──┼─>│ WORKFLOW │───>┼─ a webhook call
a web page or form ───┤  ╰──────────╯    ├─ a filled form
the Chrome side panel ╯                  ╰─ a published site
figure.alt: Five starts lead into a workflow: a person presses Run, a schedule, a webhook, a web page or form, the Chrome side panel. Five ends lead out: a result page, an email, a webhook call, a filled form, a published site.

steps.label: Starts
steps.text: 5 things start a run: a person, a clock, another system, a web page or the browser's side panel.

steps.label: Workflow
steps.text: The same workflow runs, whatever started it.

steps.label: Ends
steps.text: The result goes where it is needed: a page, a mailbox, another system, a form or a published site.

sections.title: Team
body: The agent's instructions come in layers: a neutral core, then the organisation's own rules, then the rules of each group the person belongs to. So it uses the team's words and knows the team's systems.
Groups form a tree. A workflow is shared with people or groups as viewer, runner, editor or owner, and a copy can pull changes from its parent or offer its own back.
Accounts are passkeys only, by invitation. Spending has a monthly cap for the site and for each person, and the audit log cannot be edited.

figure.alt: A sheet of an HR office's rules above the agent's reply that follows them.

sections.title: For agents
body: What a person can do on the page is a tool in one registry of 91. The chat agent and MCP clients such as Claude Code and Codex call the same tools, with the same permissions.
22 of them work on the page only: accounts, permissions and the agent's own instructions stay with a person.

sections.title: How it is built
body: The web app holds the canvas, the chat, the tools and the scheduler. Work runs in 3 kinds of runner: Python, a browser (Playwright) and office documents (LibreOffice and OCR).
Runners pull jobs from the web app and never reach the database. Each job runs in a new sandbox with a private temporary folder and no privileges.
Credentials are sealed at rest and masked in every log. The model is any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, chosen in configuration.

wide: browser      Chrome panel      Claude Code, Codex
figure.alt: A browser, the Chrome side panel and MCP clients reach the web app. The web app stores state in Postgres, hands jobs to three runners (Python, browser, documents) and calls a model gateway.

steps.label: Clients
steps.text: People use the browser or the Chrome side panel. Agents come in over MCP.

steps.label: Web app
steps.text: One web app holds the canvas, the chat, the tools and the scheduler.

steps.label: Postgres
steps.text: State lives in Postgres. Only the web app talks to it.

steps.label: Runners
steps.text: Runners pull jobs and run each one in a fresh sandbox.

steps.label: Models
steps.text: AI steps call one model endpoint, chosen in configuration.

name: Carrel
purpose: lab machines, asked for in words
intro: A carrel is the desk a library sets aside for one graduate student. Carrel gives every WinLab member their own corner of the lab's Proxmox VE cluster.
Members never touch Proxmox. They tell their agent what machine they need, and one MCP endpoint creates it and returns an SSH line.
From there the same endpoint gives the machine a domain, opens its ports and deploys its code on every push.

sections.title: Ask for a machine
body: The member says what the machine is for. The agent picks an image and a size, calls one tool and waits for the answer.

The answer comes when the machine is ready to use: it has booted, initialized and answered over SSH. In our own test that took 29 seconds. The agent writes the SSH alias into the member's config, so the next line just works.

wide: │ > Open a VM on winlab for my SDN homework                  │
│   Ready: 2 vCPU, 2 GiB RAM, 20 GiB disk.                   │
narrow: │ > Open a VM on winlab for  │
figure.alt: A Claude Code session. The member asks for a VM for SDN homework. Carrel's machine_create tool answers that the machine is ready with 2 vCPU, 2 GiB RAM and a 20 GiB disk, and gives the line ssh sdn-hw.alice.

steps.label: Ask
lit: > Open a VM on winlab for my SDN homework
> Open a VM on winlab for
steps.text: The member says what the machine is for.

steps.label: Call
steps.text: The agent picks an image and a size, and calls one tool.

steps.label: Ready
lit: Ready: 2 vCPU, 2 GiB RAM, 20 GiB disk.
steps.text: Carrel answers once the machine has booted and answered over SSH.

steps.label: Connect
steps.text: The alias is already in the member's SSH config.

sections.title: A desk of your own
body: Every member gets the same budget, and spends it as they like: 8 small machines, or one large one. A project group gets a second budget of its own.
A machine is a full VM (Debian or Ubuntu, with Docker and cloud-init) or a lighter container. Each member also has private networks, so machines talk to each other and to nobody else.

wide: 1 GiB    2 GiB      8 GiB          16 GiB of memory
10 GiB   20 GiB     40 GiB         80 GiB of disk
figure.alt: Four machine sizes drawn as boxes that double in width: tiny with 1 vCPU, 1 GiB of memory and 10 GiB of disk, small with 2, 2 and 20, medium with 4, 8 and 40, large with 8, 16 and 80.

steps.label: Tiny
steps.text: The default: enough for a bot or a small service.

steps.label: Small
steps.text: A prepared development machine starts here.

steps.label: Medium
steps.text: For builds, Docker stacks and databases.

steps.label: Large
steps.text: A member's whole CPU and memory budget in one machine.

points.text: 8, with 8 vCPU, 16 GiB of memory and 100 GiB of disk between them.
10 domains under the member's own name, with HTTPS.
10 public TCP or UDP ports.
4 private networks.
4 per machine.

sections.title: Publish and deploy
body: One call puts a service on the internet: a domain with a certificate, or a public port. Names outside the member's own and fixed ports go to an admin as a request.
A repository on GitHub links to a machine once. After that every push builds, switches the machine to the new release and watches its health for 60 seconds. A failing release rolls back by itself.

wide: your repo       GitHub          the machine,    60 s of health
on GitHub       Actions         new release     or roll back
figure.alt: Four steps in a row: git push to your repository, GitHub Actions builds, the machine switches to the new release, then 60 seconds of health checks decide whether to keep it or roll back.

steps.label: Push
steps.text: A push to the linked branch starts it.

steps.label: Build
steps.text: GitHub Actions builds the release.

steps.label: Switch
steps.text: A small daemon on the machine swaps to it.

steps.label: Check
steps.text: It watches health for 60 seconds, and goes back if the release fails.

sections.title: Keep, pause, put away
body: A machine does not have to run to be kept. What a member is not using stops counting against the cluster, and comes back as it was.

points.text: Saves the disk, and rolls back to it.
Holds a VM in memory and resumes it where it stopped.
Moves a stopped machine to backup storage. Thaw restores it with the same name and address.
Changes CPU, memory and disk.
A WireGuard profile into the member's private networks.
A link to the machine's screen in the browser, when SSH is not enough.

sections.title: How it is built
body: The control plane is one Go service. It serves MCP, signs members in with the lab's Keycloak account, checks every request against the quota and runs it as a durable job, so a dropped connection never loses a machine.
Under it are the cluster's own parts: Proxmox VE for machines, EVPN and VXLAN for each member's networks, and Caddy for HTTPS. A reconciler compares the cluster with the records every 5 minutes.

wide: │ MCP over HTTPS, signed in with Keycloak
│ VMs and CTs  │ │ WireGuard    │ │ TCP and UDP  │
figure.alt: An agent reaches the Carrel control plane over MCP. The control plane, written in Go, drives three things: Proxmox VE with 4 nodes, the network (EVPN, VXLAN, WireGuard) and the gateway (Caddy for HTTPS, plus TCP and UDP ports).

steps.label: Agent
lit: MCP over HTTPS, signed in with Keycloak
steps.text: The member's agent calls one MCP endpoint, signed in with the lab account.

steps.label: Control plane
steps.text: It checks the quota, then runs the request as a durable job.

steps.label: Proxmox
steps.text: Machines are VMs and containers on 4 Proxmox VE nodes.

steps.label: Network
steps.text: Each member's networks are their own, across every node.

steps.label: Gateway
steps.text: The gateway gives services a name, a certificate and public ports.

sections.title: In numbers
body: Carrel has run the lab's machines since October 2026. These are from its public status page on 2026-11-12.

points.text: 4 nodes with 160 CPU threads, 503 GiB of memory and 2,125 GiB of disk.
30 machines for 11 accounts.
84 MCP tools: 66 for members and 18 for admins.

name: Golem
intro: Golem watches every service I run. It reads their logs, traces and metrics from Sensorium, probes their URLs and checks disks and backups.
When something breaks, it opens an incident and sends a short explanation to Telegram and to signed webhooks. When the problem goes away, it closes the incident by itself.
For a known fix, it writes a plan, asks for approval in Telegram, runs the fix and checks that the alert has cleared. Agents add new rules over MCP.

name: Good
purpose: a digital 乖乖 for servers
intro: 乖乖 is a corn snack that engineers in Taiwan tape onto servers for luck. The green bag means everything keeps running.
Good is the digital version: a 3D bag on a web page, for machines that have no shelf to put one on.

name: Plump
intro: Plump turns a flat SVG into a 3D object. You shape the depth and bevel, pick a material and light the scene.
The scene saves as a file you can open again and keep editing. The zyx mark on this site's earlier home page was made with it.

name: UI
intro: The design system behind every zyx.tw site: grayscale tokens and our own components on Base UI, served as a shadcn registry.
It sets a terminal look with one monospace face, 4 type sizes, square corners and 2 motion durations. A token check in CI blocks values outside the system.

name: Sensorium
intro: My services already speak OpenTelemetry, but the reader of their logs at 3 am is often an agent now. Sensorium keeps the logs, traces and metrics of many services in one Postgres store.
Agents read them through 8 MCP tools, so "what broke?" is one tool call. Each project has its own ingest token, and old data expires by itself.

name: NYCU AI
intro: The official website of NYCU's Office of AI Affairs, with its news, events and programs.
Content lives in Postgres and is edited in the browser, and the site serves an MCP endpoint so agents can read it.

name: WinLab
intro: The public website of the Wireless Internet Laboratory at NYCU, led by Prof. Chien-Chao Tseng.
One page covers the lab's research areas, from SDN and 5G/6G orchestration to cloud-native systems, with a link to the members' portal.

name: WinLab Portal
intro: WinLab members book rooms, file receipts, sign documents, order meals and open the lab door through one portal.
Every action is defined once, so a member can click it and an agent can call it as an MCP tool. Members sign in with the lab's Keycloak account.

name: WinLab Video
intro: The lab's video library. Members sign in to watch, and the site remembers where each viewer stopped.
Videos stream from the lab's Nextcloud, and each upload gets a transcript beside the player that jumps to the spoken line.

name: Link
intro: Paste a long URL, get a short one back. That is all it does.

name: Time
intro: What time is it? A clock, that's all.
